turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Come on through, Mia. We'll grab your obs before Dr Khan sees you. Your mum can stay.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah nah, this is a waste of an arvo. I'm fine.
[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She's not fine, love. Just sit.
[SEG0004] person_1 (NURSE): Arm out for me. Sorry if I yawn, my little boy's been home all week with a crook tummy and I barely slept.
[SEG0005] person_1 (NURSE): Right. Pulse is a hundred and eighteen. Blood pressure one twenty eight over seventy four. Oxygen sats ninety nine percent.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): A hundred and eighteen's nothing. I walked in from the car park.
[SEG0007] person_1 (NURSE): Mm. He'll be along in a tick.
[SEG0008] person_4 (DOCTOR): G'day Mia, I'm Dr Khan. Hello, you're mum I take it. What's brought you in?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Mum dragged me. I've dropped a bit of weight, that's all. Nothing dramatic.
[SEG0010] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It's not a bit. Her jeans are hanging off her. It started about two months ago.
[SEG0011] person_4 (DOCTOR): No rush. Mia, in your own words, how much, and over how long?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm. Six or seven kilos, over two months. I wasn't dieting or anything. It's fine.
[SEG0013] person_4 (DOCTOR): And the appetite, while that's been happening?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Eating more, actually. Hungry all the time. Still losing it, which is... anyway. I don't really care.
[SEG0015] person_4 (DOCTOR): Tell me about your heart. Any racing, any thumping?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Goes a bit quick sometimes. Mostly when I'm just sitting. I ignore it.
[SEG0017] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Last night on the couch her neck was pulsing. She said it felt like it was banging in her chest.
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, alright, it bangs a bit. Not dying.
[SEG0019] person_4 (DOCTOR): What about sweating?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): A bit clammy at night. I'll blame summer. It's only mild.
[SEG0021] person_4 (DOCTOR): And your hands, have they been shaky?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, a little. When I hold a cup. Half the time I don't even clock it.
[SEG0023] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain when it races?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Nah. No chest pain.
[SEG0025] person_4 (DOCTOR): Short of breath at all?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I'm on my feet all day at work in the warehouse, and I'm sweet.
[SEG0027] person_4 (DOCTOR): Bowels? Any diarrhoea or tummy pain?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Tummy's good. No diarrhoea.
[SEG0029] person_4 (DOCTOR): Fevers?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever. I'm a bit tired in the arvo, but everyone is.
[SEG0031] person_4 (DOCTOR): How's sleep?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Sleep's fine. I'm out like a light.

[SEG0033] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): You need to tell him about Jess. That's her older sister. She's got thyroid disease, the overactive kind. Been on carbinazole for years, I never say that name right.
[SEG0034] person_4 (DOCTOR): That's useful, thank you. Mia, you knew it was in the family?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, Jess has it. I don't. I'm nothing like her.
[SEG0036] person_4 (DOCTOR): Mind if I have a look? Hands out flat, palms down.

[SEG0037] person_4 (DOCTOR): There's a fine tremor in both hands. Pulse is rapid and regular, matching that hundred and eighteen. And the thyroid in your neck feels mildly enlarged, smooth, no nodules.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Enlarged. Right. It's probably just my neck.

[SEG0039] person_4 (DOCTOR): I know you want to wave it away. My working impression is an overactive thyroid, thyrotoxicosis. The gland is releasing too much hormone and that runs the body in fast forward, so the heart speeds up, you lose weight even while eating more, the hands shake and you sweat. That's the mechanism, not you being precious.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): So I'm turning into Jess. Fantastic.
[SEG0041] person_4 (DOCTOR): Not proven today, it's just where I'm leaning. I won't start any tablets until we see the bloods.
[SEG0042] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): So what are you actually doing?
[SEG0043] person_4 (DOCTOR): Bloods today. tsh and free t three, uh, free t four, and a full blood count. Plus an ecg before you go, with that heart rate.

[SEG0044] person_1 (NURSE): I can do the ecg in the side room and take the bloods after. My sister had her thyroid taken out last year, so I know the word freaks people out. That's her story though, not yours, Mia.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Ecg's over the top. I'll do it, whatever.

[SEG0046] person_4 (DOCTOR): It only takes a few minutes and it shows the rhythm. If the coffees are stacking up, ease right off, they stir the heart up. And if you get chest pain, or you faint, don't minimise that, get seen straight away.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): I have, err, four long blacks a day. Used to be more, nah, four. I'll cut back, probably.
[SEG0048] person_4 (DOCTOR): Good. Reception will book you back with me in one week for the results. That visit happens either way, not only if you feel worse.
[SEG0049] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll get her here.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah yeah. We finished?
[SEG0051] person_1 (NURSE): Nearly. Come with me for the ecg and the bloods, then you're free. No worries.

spec.situation: Younger adult losing weight with a fast heartbeat, sweating, shaky hands, eats more than usual; hair thinning not mentioned; a sister has thyroid disease; blood tests and ECG planned.

traps.happens: The doctor (or nurse) explains a mechanism or a diagnosis in the patient's body ('the voice box is irritated by reflux', 'diabetes dulls the nerves in the feet', 'the swelling is your body fighting infection'). A nurse or caregiver also mentions a fact about THEIR OWN life (their sister, their child, their own illness).
traps.label_rule: Explanations by the doctor are NEVER symptoms, history or social history of the patient; they may only appear as clinical_assessment or counselling if the doctor stated them as such. A nurse's or caregiver's own life facts are not recorded as the patient's. Each symptom's reported_by is the person who really described it.

features: doctor_misses_topics: the doctor does not ask about everything; topics never discussed are simply absent (no invented denials, no allergy line if allergies were never mentioned).

spoken_numbers: doses, vitals and durations are spoken as words or sloppy speech ('a hundred and two point five', 'one-forty over ninety', 'five-ish years', 'twenty milligram'); the label writes them normally (102.5, 140/90, 20 mg) and does not turn vague ones into exact ones.

bad.reason: Transcript supports mild sweating at night, not specifically "night sweats."
bad.text: Night sweats (category=constitutional, status=present, severity=mild, frequency=at night, temporality=current, reported_by=patient, certainty=certain)

bad.reason: Provisional thyrotoxicosis is stated, but family history basis came from sister, not explicitly cited by doctor.
bad.text: Overactive thyroid, thyrotoxicosis (certainty=provisional, basis=Weight loss despite eating more, palpitations, night sweats, shaky hands, sister with overactive thyroid, and examination, stated_by=doctor)

omissions.text: Weight loss amount was six or seven kilograms over two months, not just unspecified weight loss.
Palpitations/heart racing occur even while she is just sitting, and family reported last night her neck was visibly pulsing and she said it felt like it was banging in her chest.
Doctor said he would not start any tablets until the blood results are back.
Planned blood tests included free T3 as well as TSH, free T4, and full blood count.

Safety-net advice included seeking urgent review if she faints/syncope occurs; recorded facts mention fainting but not that this was specifically discussed as a red-flag symptom to get seen straight away.
Follow-up instruction was to return in one week for results regardless of whether symptoms worsen, not only if she feels worse.
